claims.arxiv2604_09101: When an outside provider adapts a CLIP image classifier by prompt tuning and leaves both encoders frozen, an auditor can examine the delivered model before deployment, tell whether it carries a backdoor, and name the class the attacker targeted. Detection counts only if, at a decision threshold of 2 fixed in advance, the auditor separates clean from backdoored models with higher model-level AUROC and names the target class with higher F1 than the strongest earlier model-level detector, while spending no more optimisation than that detector. A follow-up repair of a flagged model counts only if it brings the backdoor's attack success rate below 10% while keeping clean top-1 accuracy within one percentage point of its value before repair.
claims.arxiv2604_09101_c1: A model-level backdoor audit of CLIP classifiers still works against an attacker who deliberately narrows the trigger so that only the exact pattern fires, and against backdoors planted in a fine-tuned image encoder instead of a prompt-tuning module. A backdoor counts as caught only when the model's anomaly score reaches 2 and the audit's recovered trigger achieves at least 50% attack success. Supported only if the audit catches a majority of the narrowed-trigger backdoors and every encoder-level backdoor tested.

0.text: Assemble clean and backdoored models to audit. Setup: CLIP ViT-B/16 prompt-tuned with CoCoOp (encoders frozen) on the seen classes of ten datasets (ImageNet, Caltech101, OxfordPets, Flowers102, Food101, FGVC Aircraft, SUN397, DTD, EuroSAT, UCF101); per dataset one clean model and four backdoored ones (BadCLIP, plus Blended, SIBA and WaNet adapted to prompt tuning, 10% poisoning), 50 models in all. Result: backdoored models keep clean accuracy close to the clean models (about 82% seen-class) with high attack success (BadCLIP about 99% seen, 97% unseen; SIBA weakest at about 66%/52%).

2.text: Head-to-head detection. Setup: for every one of the 50 models, a 50-label candidate set that contains the true target, 1,000 unlabeled Open Images photos with no class overlap, and three detectors run on identical inputs: the audit (one epoch, roughly 32 updates per class) versus Neural Cleanse and Pixel Backdoor (five epochs each, original losses). Threshold k=2 for all. Measured: model-level accuracy and AUROC, target-class F1, run time. Result: 47/50 models correct (94%), AUROC 0.973 versus 0.495 (Neural Cleanse) and 0.687 (Pixel Backdoor); target-class F1 0.92 versus 0.06 and 0.42, with almost no false-positive classes; a 50-class scan takes under an hour on one A100 versus 6 and 8 hours. The three misses are the clean FGVC model, DTD-WaNet and EuroSAT-BadCLIP.

3.text: Does the score single out the target class, rather than any class being easy to attack? Setup: on Caltech101, compare the recovered-trigger attack success and optimisation loss for the target class against the highest non-target class, for the clean model and each attack. Result: for the audit, the target class stands far above every other class in backdoored models (gaps of roughly 50-73 points in attack success) and not in the clean model; Neural Cleanse recovers near-100% triggers for clean and backdoored models alike, and Pixel Backdoor 86-97%, so their scores do not separate the cases.

7.text: Detection against an attacker who knows the audit. Setup: a two-phase BadCLIP variant that first learns a trigger, then trains the model to fire only on that exact trigger and to ignore noisy approximations of it, which is what inversion recovers. Result: the attack itself weakens (seen-class success about 64% instead of 99%); recovered triggers drop to about 70% success; the audit still flags 8 of 10 adaptive models, missing EuroSAT (anomaly score 1.66, under 2) and UCF101 (recovered trigger only 31% successful, treated as invalid).

8.text: Repair using the recovered trigger. Setup: take the class with the top anomaly score, stamp its recovered trigger onto a small labelled clean set while keeping the true labels, and fine-tune CoCoOp-style. Measured: clean accuracy and attack success before and after, averaged over ten datasets. Result: attack success falls below 10% for every attack (84.4% to 6.1% overall; BadCLIP 98.5% to 7.6%); clean accuracy moves from 80.6% to 80.8% overall, within one point for every attack except SIBA, which rises by about two points (75.9% to 77.9%).

9.text: Is it the recovered trigger that repairs, or just fine-tuning? Setup: same repair with clean-only data, with random bounded noise, with the trigger recovered for a wrong class, and with the target-class trigger. Result: final attack success 64.6% (clean-only), 52.7% (random noise), 47.0% (wrong-class trigger) versus 6.1% with the target-class trigger, at similar clean accuracy; only SIBA is also removed by the wrong-class trigger.

10.text: Does the audit find backdoors outside the prompt module? Setup: fully fine-tune CLIP's image encoder with Blended poisoning (no prompt module at all) using three trigger patterns (noise patch, triangle, text) and run the audit unchanged. Result: all three poisoned models are flagged, with anomaly scores 6.15, 5.93 and 4.38 and recovered triggers reaching 99%, 97% and 62% attack success.

notes: Full paper seen in v3. Corrected [8]: v3 omitted that SIBA's clean accuracy rises by ~2 points, outside the claim's +-1 pp repair bar. [7] now states that the attack itself weakens.
